relationship: related use of parables to address Israel
rationale: Ezekiel is commanded to tell a story and speak a parable to Israel's house. The psalm addresses the people and announces speech in parables and ancient riddles. The literary method corresponds; the psalm recounts ancestral testimony rather than this eagle-and-vine story.
source_text: “Son of man, tell a story and speak a parable to the house of Israel,

target_units.text: Of understanding. Of Asaph. Attend, my people, to my law; bend your ear to the words of my mouth.
I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter riddles from the beginning,
whatever we heard and knew, and our fathers recounted to us,
it was not hidden from their children for another generation, as we announce the Lord’s praises, His mighty acts and the wonders He did.

relationship: same-chapter interpretation of the conquering eagle
rationale: The great eagle takes the cedar's choice parts. The explanation asks whether the audience understands the story and describes Babylon's king taking Jerusalem's king and rulers. This follows the chapter's own movement from political imagery to its stated interpretation.
source_text: and say, ‘Thus says the Lord: The great eagle, with great wings and a broad span, full of talons, which has authority to enter Lebanon, took the cedar’s choice parts;

target_units.text: “Son of man, say now to the embittering house, ‘Do you not understand what these things were?’ Say, ‘When Babylon’s king comes against Jerusalem, he will take her king and her rulers and bring them to himself in Babylon.

relationship: same-chapter interpretation of the removed cedar growth
rationale: The eagle carries the tender growth to Canaan and a fortified city. The explanation describes Jerusalem's king and rulers being brought to Babylon. The literary correspondence is retained while preserving the parable's actual Canaan wording rather than silently replacing it with Babylon.
source_text: he nipped off the tips of its tender growth, carried them to the land of Canaan, and set them in a fortified city.

target_units.text: “Son of man, say now to the embittering house, ‘Do you not understand what these things were?’ Say, ‘When Babylon’s king comes against Jerusalem, he will take her king and her rulers and bring them to himself in Babylon.

relationship: same-chapter royal interpretation of the planted seed
rationale: The eagle plants seed from the land under supervision. The explanation describes taking royal seed, imposing a covenant and establishing a weak kingdom. The connection concerns the parable's planted seed and the explicitly named royal seed, without importing a personal name.
source_text: He took some of the land’s seed and put it in the plain, a plant beside abundant water; he appointed it to be watched over.

target_units.text: He will take one of the royal seed, make a covenant with him, and bring him under a curse-oath. He will take the land’s leaders,
so that it may become a weak kingdom, not exalt itself at all, and keep his covenant and establish it.

relationship: same-chapter correspondence between the weak vine and weak kingdom
rationale: The growing vine is expressly weak and small. The explanation likewise says the kingdom is to remain weak rather than exalt itself, preserving the covenant. This close weakness correspondence helps explain the plant image without asserting that every botanical detail has a separately stated political equivalent.
source_text: It sprouted and became a weak vine, small in size so that it might appear. Its branches were upon it and its roots beneath it. It became a vine, produced offshoots and extended its climbing growth.

target_units.text: so that it may become a weak kingdom, not exalt itself at all, and keep his covenant and establish it.

relationship: same-chapter explanation of turning toward a second protector
rationale: The vine directs roots and branches toward another eagle for water. The explanation describes revolt and seeking Egypt's horses and people. The second appeal for support is the particular common movement.
source_text: There was another great eagle, with great wings and many talons. Behold, this vine was intertwined toward him, its roots toward him; it sent its branches to him to water it together with the clod of its planting.

target_units.text: He will revolt from him, sending his messengers to Egypt to give him horses and many people. Will he prosper? Will the one doing contrary things be rescued? Will one transgressing a covenant be saved?
As I live, says the Lord, surely in the place of the king who made him king—he who dishonored My curse-oath and transgressed My covenant—with him in the midst of Babylon he will die.
Pharaoh will not wage war against him with great power or a numerous crowd, amid siegeworks and the building of missile stations to remove lives.

relationship: related flourishing national vine imagery
rationale: The parable describes a vine flourishing in a good plain, with shoots and fruit. The psalm depicts Israel through a transplanted vine whose roots fill the land and whose branches spread widely. The psalm does not supply the source's abundant-water or fruit clauses.
source_text: It grows fat in a good plain beside abundant water, to produce shoots, bear fruit and become a great vine.

target_units.text: Thou didst transplant a vine from Egypt; Thou didst cast out nations and plant her.
Thou madest a road before her and didst plant her roots, and the land was filled.
Her shadow covered mountains, and her climbing branches covered God’s cedars.
She stretched her branches as far as the sea, and her offshoots as far as the River.

relationship: related judgment expressed through ruined roots and lost fruit
rationale: The vine's roots and fruit rot and its early shoots dry up. Hosea describes Ephraim drying at the roots and no longer bearing fruit. The plant images both portray national ruin, with rotting in Ezekiel and drying explicitly named in Hosea.
source_text: Therefore say, ‘Thus says the Lord: Will it prosper? Will not the roots of its tender growth and its fruit rot, and all its early shoots dry up? No great arm or numerous people will be needed to pull it from its roots.

target_units.text: Ephraim suffered; he dried up at his roots; he will certainly bear fruit no longer. Even if they give birth, I will kill the desired offspring of their womb.

relationship: close vine-destruction imagery involving a scorching wind
rationale: Both parables describe the scorching wind drying the plant's growth. The source says the vine dries with the clod of its growth; the later lament also describes wrath, being thrown down and consuming fire. Those additional actions are not inserted into the source.
source_text: Behold, it grows fat—surely it will not prosper? Will it not dry up completely as soon as the scorching wind touches it? It will dry up together with the clod of its growth.’”

target_units.text: She was broken off in wrath and thrown to the ground. The scorching wind dried her choice parts; her rod of strength was punished and dried up. Fire consumed her.

relationship: related removal of a Judean king to Babylon before another appointment
rationale: The explanation predicts Babylon's king taking Jerusalem's king and rulers. Chronicles narrates Nebuchadnezzar bringing Jechonias to Babylon and appointing Zedekiah. The source leaves its king unnamed, so the comparison does not turn the target's names into names supplied by Ezekiel.
source_text: “Son of man, say now to the embittering house, ‘Do you not understand what these things were?’ Say, ‘When Babylon’s king comes against Jerusalem, he will take her king and her rulers and bring them to himself in Babylon.

target_units.text: Jechonias was eighteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned three months and ten days in Jerusalem. He did what was evil before the Lord.
At the turn of the year King Nebuchadnezzar sent and brought him into Babylon with the desirable vessels of the Lord’s house. He made Zedekiah, his father’s brother, king over Judah and Jerusalem.

relationship: close counterpart for a Babylonian-imposed royal oath
rationale: Ezekiel describes Babylon's king binding royal seed by covenant and a curse-oath. Chronicles says Nebuchadnezzar made Zedekiah swear by God and records his breach of obligation. The named narrative is a particular comparison; the source itself does not name its oath-taker.
source_text: He will take one of the royal seed, make a covenant with him, and bring him under a curse-oath. He will take the land’s leaders,

target_units.text: in breaking his obligations to King Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God. He hardened his neck and strengthened his heart so as not to return to the Lord God of Israel.

relationship: related weakening of Judah through removal of its powerful people
rationale: The source explains the preceding removal of leaders as establishing a weak kingdom. Kings describes deportation of rulers, powerful men, warriors and craftsmen, leaving the poor. The target supplies a narrated loss of strength but does not state this source's covenant condition.
source_text: so that it may become a weak kingdom, not exalt itself at all, and keep his covenant and establish it.

target_units.text: He deported Jerusalem, all the rulers, and the mighty in strength, taking ten thousand captives, and every craftsman and one who shuts up. None remained except the land’s poor.
He deported Joakim to Babylon, along with the king’s mother, the king’s wives, and his eunuchs. He led the land’s powerful men into deportation from Jerusalem to Babylon,
and all the men of the force, seven thousand, and the craftsmen and those who shut up, one thousand—all mighty men who waged war. The king of Babylon brought them into deportation to Babylon.

relationship: close warning against reliance on Egyptian military help
rationale: The ruler seeks horses and many people from Egypt, and his hope of rescue is challenged. Isaiah rebukes seeking Egypt's horses and chariots instead of God and predicts the helpers' failure. Ezekiel additionally identifies revolt and a broken covenant.
source_text: He will revolt from him, sending his messengers to Egypt to give him horses and many people. Will he prosper? Will the one doing contrary things be rescued? Will one transgressing a covenant be saved?

target_units.text: Woe to those going down to Egypt for help, trusting in horses and chariots because there are many, and in horses, a very great multitude, but not trusting Israel’s Holy One or seeking God!
He Himself, wise, brought evils upon them; His word will certainly not be set aside. He will rise against evil people’s houses and against their futile hope,
an Egyptian human being and not God, horses’ flesh, with no help. The Lord will bring His hand against them; the helpers will grow weary, and all will perish together.

relationship: related death in Babylon of a defeated Judean ruler
rationale: Ezekiel predicts that the oath-breaking ruler will die with the king who installed him in Babylon. Jeremiah records Zedekiah being brought to Babylon and held in a mill house until death. The narrative supplies a named counterpart without making Ezekiel's unnamed ruler explicitly named in the source.
source_text: As I live, says the Lord, surely in the place of the king who made him king—he who dishonored My curse-oath and transgressed My covenant—with him in the midst of Babylon he will die.

target_units.text: He blinded Zedekiah’s eyes and bound him in fetters. The king of Babylon brought him to Babylon and put him in a mill house until the day he died.

relationship: related warnings concerning Pharaoh's military role during Jerusalem's siege
rationale: Following the request for Egyptian horses and manpower, Ezekiel says Pharaoh will not wage war against him with great power amid siege operations. Jeremiah explicitly says the Egyptian force that came to help will return home and the Chaldeans will return to capture Jerusalem. The source's ambiguous against him is not resolved into the target's express help-and-withdrawal description.
source_text: Pharaoh will not wage war against him with great power or a numerous crowd, amid siegeworks and the building of missile stations to remove lives.

target_units.text: Thus said the Lord: Tell Judah’s king, who sent to you to seek Me, Pharaoh’s force, which came out to help you, will return to Egypt’s land.
The Chaldeans themselves will return, fight this city, seize it, and burn it with fire.

relationship: contrast between violating and preserving a binding sworn covenant
rationale: Ezekiel condemns a dishonored oath and transgressed covenant, denying escape. Joshua's leaders refuse to attack those to whom they swore by the Lord, specifically to avoid wrath for the oath. The parties differ, while the binding force of the sworn undertaking is explicit in both.
source_text: He dishonored a sworn oath by transgressing a covenant; behold, he has given his hand and did all these things to him. Surely he will not be saved?

target_units.text: The sons of Israel did not fight them, because all the leaders had sworn to them by the Lord, the God of Israel. The whole congregation grumbled against the leaders.
The leaders said to the whole congregation, “We have sworn to them by the Lord, the God of Israel, and now we cannot touch them.
This is what we shall do: keep them alive and preserve them, so that wrath does not come against us because of the oath we swore to them.

relationship: related divine judgment for dishonoring an oath in God's name
rationale: The Lord says He will bring the dishonored oath and broken covenant upon the ruler's head. Zechariah's curse punishes false swearers and enters the house of one who swears falsely by God's name. The target describes a household's destruction rather than the source's royal fate.
source_text: Therefore say, ‘Thus says the Lord: As I live, surely My covenant that he transgressed and My sworn oath that he dishonored—I will bring them upon his head.

target_units.text: He said to me, “This is the curse going out over the whole earth, because every thief will be punished by this with death, and every false swearer will be punished by this with death.

I will bring it out, says the Lord Almighty. It will enter the thief’s house and the house of whoever swears falsely by My name; it will lodge within his house and destroy it completely, its timbers and its stones.”

relationship: close divine net-and-enclosure image of capture
rationale: Both declarations say God will spread His net over the ruler and that he will be caught in an enclosure. This source says his enclosure; the target says My enclosure and additionally predicts deportation to Babylon. The possessive and added destination are preserved.
source_text: I will spread My net over him, and he will be caught in his enclosure.

target_units.text: I will spread My net over him, and he will be caught in My enclosure. I will bring him to Babylon, to the Chaldeans’ land, and he will not see it, and there he will die.

relationship: close sword and scattering of a ruler's supporters
rationale: The source predicts death by sword among the ruler's battle array and scattering of survivors to every wind. The target describes his helpers and supporters scattered to every wind with a sword drawn after them. Both connect the ruler's fall with dispersal of those around him.
source_text: In all his battle array they will fall by the sword, and I will scatter the survivors to every wind. You will recognize that I, the Lord, have spoken.’

target_units.text: All those around him, his helpers and all who support him, I will scatter to every wind; I will draw a sword after them.

relationship: same-chapter reversal of the taking of choice cedar growth
rationale: The eagle takes the cedar's choice parts and carries its tender growth away. God now takes choice cedar material and plants it on a high mountain. The repeated cedar-taking image supports this reversal without identifying the later plant as a specifically named king or replacing the source's unusual top-of-their-heart wording.
source_text: For thus says the Lord: I Myself will take from the cedar’s choice parts, nip off from the top of their heart, and I Myself will plant it upon a high mountain. I will suspend it

target_units.text: and say, ‘Thus says the Lord: The great eagle, with great wings and a broad span, full of talons, which has authority to enter Lebanon, took the cedar’s choice parts;
he nipped off the tips of its tender growth, carried them to the land of Canaan, and set them in a fortified city.

relationship: related plant imagery sheltering birds beneath its shade
rationale: The planted cedar grows and shelters birds under its shade, as well as beasts beneath it. Jesus' kingdom parable describes a mustard plant with great branches under whose shade birds can shelter. The plant species and the source's additional beasts remain distinct.
source_text: upon Israel’s lofty mountain and plant it. It will produce a shoot, bear fruit and become a great cedar. Every beast will rest beneath it, every bird will rest under its shade, and its branches will be restored.

target_units.text: He said, “How shall we compare the kingdom of God, or in what parable shall we set it out?
It is like a mustard seed, which, when sown on the ground, is smaller than all the seeds on the earth.
Yet when sown, it grows up and becomes larger than all the garden plants, and makes great branches, so that the birds of the sky can shelter under its shade.”

relationship: close divine reversal of high and low conditions
rationale: God lowers the high tree and raises the low, also reversing green and dry growth. Hannah's song says the Lord humbles and raises high and lifts the poor to sit with rulers. The target supports the reversal of rank without supplying the source's botanical details.
source_text: All the plain’s trees will know that I am the Lord who lowers a high tree, raises a low tree, dries a green tree and makes a dry tree flourish. I, the Lord, have spoken and will act.”

target_units.text: The Lord makes poor and makes rich; He humbles and raises high.
He raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dung heap, to seat them with rulers of peoples and grant them a throne of glory as their inheritance,

relationship: close shared proverb about unripe grapes and children's teeth
rationale: Ezekiel quotes the proverb attributing children's affected teeth to their fathers' eating. Jeremiah quotes the same proverb and says it will cease, replacing it with each person's own sin and eating. Both passages challenge this proverb's use to explain responsibility.
source_text: “Son of man, what is this proverb you have among Israel’s sons, saying, ‘The fathers ate unripe grapes, and the children’s teeth were set on edge’?

target_units.text: In those days they will certainly not say: The fathers ate an unripe grape, and the children’s teeth were set on edge.
Instead, each will die in his own sin, and the one eating the unripe grape will have his own teeth set on edge.

relationship: close announced end of the inherited-grape proverb
rationale: The Lord swears that the proverb will no longer be spoken in Israel. Jeremiah likewise announces days when people will not say that fathers ate an unripe grape and children's teeth were set on edge. The target states the proverb rather than leaving it in the preceding unit.
source_text: As I live, says the Lord, this proverb will certainly no longer be spoken in Israel.

target_units.text: In those days they will certainly not say: The fathers ate an unripe grape, and the children’s teeth were set on edge.

relationship: close individual responsibility for the sin that brings death
rationale: Ezekiel says father and son belong to God and the soul that sins will die. Deuteronomy says fathers and sons must not die for each other and each dies for his own sin. The law does not include the source's express divine ownership of all souls.
source_text: For all souls are Mine. As the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son—they are Mine. The soul that sins will die.

target_units.text: Fathers shall not die for children, and sons shall not die for fathers. Each shall die for his own sin.

relationship: related practice of justice as the path to life
rationale: Ezekiel introduces the righteous person as practicing judgment and righteousness, with life promised at the conclusion of the description. Deuteronomy commands pursuing what is just justly so that the people may live and inherit the land. The source then develops a fuller catalogue of conduct.
source_text: The person who is righteous, practicing judgment and righteousness,

target_units.text: You shall pursue justly that which is just, that you may live, and enter and inherit the land which the Lord your God gives you.

relationship: close prohibitions concerning a neighbor's wife and menstrual separation
rationale: Two of Ezekiel's defining prohibitions are defiling a neighbor's wife and approaching a woman in menstrual separation. Leviticus expressly prohibits both acts in adjacent laws. The target does not supply the source's mountain eating or reflections clauses.
source_text: will not eat upon the mountains, certainly will not raise his eyes to the reflections of the house of Israel, certainly will not defile his neighbor’s wife, and will not approach a woman in her menstrual separation;

target_units.text: And you shall not approach a woman in separation for her uncleanness to uncover her nakedness.
And you shall not lie with your neighbour’s wife to emit semen and become defiled through her.

relationship: close duty to return a debtor's pledge
rationale: Ezekiel's righteous person returns a debtor's pledge. Deuteronomy requires returning a poor debtor's pledged garment by sunset so that he can sleep in it. The target specifies the poor debtor, garment and timing not given in this source clause.
source_text: he certainly will not oppress anyone, will return a debtor’s pledge, takes no plunder, will give his bread to the hungry, and will clothe the naked;

target_units.text: And if the man is poor, you shall not sleep with his pledge in your keeping.
You shall surely restore his pledge at the setting of the sun, that he may sleep in his garment and bless you; and it shall be mercy unto you before the Lord your God.

relationship: close paired duties of feeding the hungry and clothing the naked
rationale: Ezekiel describes giving bread to the hungry and clothing the naked. Isaiah likewise commands breaking bread for the hungry and clothing the naked, alongside hospitality. This target supports the source's two charitable acts, distinct from its pledge-return requirement.
source_text: he certainly will not oppress anyone, will return a debtor’s pledge, takes no plunder, will give his bread to the hungry, and will clothe the naked;

target_units.text: Break your bread for the hungry and bring homeless poor people into your house. If you see someone naked, clothe him; do not overlook those belonging to your own family.

relationship: close prohibition of interest and increase
rationale: Ezekiel's righteous person does not lend silver at interest or take increase. Leviticus expressly forbids interest and increase from the impoverished brother and lending him silver at interest. The legal context identifies the borrower more specifically.
source_text: he will not give his silver at interest or take increase, will turn his hand from injustice, and will render a righteous judgment between a man and his neighbor;

target_units.text: You shall take no interest or increase from him, and you shall fear your God; I am the Lord; and your brother shall live with you.
You shall not give him your silver at interest or give your food for an increase.

relationship: close requirement of righteous judgment between people
rationale: Ezekiel requires righteous judgment between a man and his neighbor. Moses commands judges to judge justly between a man, his brother and the sojourner. This target supports the judicial clause rather than the separate lending prohibition.
source_text: he will not give his silver at interest or take increase, will turn his hand from injustice, and will render a righteous judgment between a man and his neighbor;

target_units.text: And I commanded your judges at that time, saying: Hear the matters between your brethren, and judge justly between a man and his brother and the sojourner with him.

relationship: close life promised through carrying out God's ordinances
rationale: Ezekiel's conclusion joins walking in God's commands and doing His ordinances with assured life. Leviticus likewise says the person who keeps and does the ordinances and judgments will live by them. The shared conduct-and-life formulation is explicit.
source_text: he has walked in My commands and kept My ordinances to carry them out. This one is righteous; he will surely live, says the Lord.

target_units.text: And you shall keep all My ordinances and all My judgments, and do them; the man who does them shall live by them; I am the Lord your God.

relationship: related example of a blood-shedding son after a righteous father
rationale: Ezekiel introduces a blood-shedding son of the righteous man. Kings describes Manasseh's abundant innocent bloodshed; the read surrounding records identify him as Hezekiah's son and describe Hezekiah's fidelity. This is an illustrative narrative comparison, not an identification of Ezekiel's hypothetical son.
source_text: But if he fathers a pestilent son who sheds blood and commits sins,

target_units.text: Manasseh also poured out very much innocent blood, until he filled Jerusalem from end to end, besides his sins by which he caused Judah to do evil in the Lord’s eyes.

relationship: close violation of the prohibition against defiling a neighbor's wife
rationale: The wicked son defiles his neighbor's wife. Leviticus directly prohibits intercourse with a neighbor's wife and calls it defilement. Ezekiel also names mountain eating and failure to follow the father, which this legal unit does not address.
source_text: he did not walk in the way of his righteous father, but even ate upon the mountains and defiled his neighbor’s wife,

target_units.text: And you shall not lie with your neighbour’s wife to emit semen and become defiled through her.

relationship: related oppression of the poor and failure to restore a pledge
rationale: The son oppresses the poor and needy and does not return a pledge. Exodus forbids pressing a poor borrower hard and requires returning a pledged garment before sunset. The source additionally lists plunder and idols, beyond the selected law.
source_text: oppressed the poor and needy, seized plunder, did not return a pledge, set his eyes upon idols, and has committed lawlessness,

target_units.text: And if you lend silver to your poor brother beside you, you shall not press him hard, neither shall you lay interest upon him.
And if you take your neighbour’s garment in pledge, you shall restore it to him before the setting of the sun;
for this is his covering, his only garment for his nakedness; What shall he sleep in? If therefore he cries to Me, I will listen to him; for I am merciful.

relationship: close breach of the interest-and-increase prohibition
rationale: The wicked son gives at interest and takes increase. Leviticus forbids those lending practices toward the poor brother. Ezekiel pronounces death and responsibility for the son's whole catalogue of lawlessness; the target itself does not prescribe that penalty for this loan.
source_text: gave at interest and took increase—this one certainly will not live. He committed all this lawlessness; he will surely be put to death, and his blood will be upon him.

target_units.text: You shall take no interest or increase from him, and you shall fear your God; I am the Lord; and your brother shall live with you.
You shall not give him your silver at interest or give your food for an increase.

relationship: related righteous son whose practice differs from his wicked father's
rationale: Ezekiel describes a son who sees his father's sins and does not repeat them. Chronicles describes Josiah pursuing God and cleansing Judah after the read account of his father Amon's idolatry. It supplies a concrete generational contrast without asserting that Chronicles narrates Ezekiel's precise seeing-and-fearing sequence.
source_text: But if he fathers a son who sees all the sins his father committed, becomes afraid, and does not act according to them,

target_units.text: Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem.
He did what was upright before the Lord and walked in the ways of his father David, turning aside neither to the right nor to the left.

In the eighth year of his reign, while still a boy, he began to seek the Lord, the God of his father David. In the twelfth year of his reign he began to cleanse Judah and Jerusalem of the high places, sacred groves, and cast objects.

relationship: close rejection of adultery with a neighbor's wife
rationale: The righteous son has not defiled his neighbor's wife. Leviticus expressly condemns adultery with that wife and assigns a penalty. The target supports that specific prohibition, not the source's separate mountain and reflections clauses.
source_text: he has not eaten upon the mountains, not set his eyes upon the reflections of the house of Israel, and not defiled his neighbor’s wife,

target_units.text: If a man commits adultery with a man’s wife, or commits adultery with his neighbour’s wife, both the adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death.

relationship: close bread-and-clothing pattern of care for the needy
rationale: Ezekiel's son gives bread to the hungry and clothes the naked. Isaiah commands the same paired acts. This comparison does not change the source's saying he has not taken a pledge into the different pledge-return wording used elsewhere.
source_text: has not oppressed anyone, not taken a pledge, and not seized plunder; he gave his bread to the hungry and clothed the naked,

target_units.text: Break your bread for the hungry and bring homeless poor people into your house. If you see someone naked, clothe him; do not overlook those belonging to your own family.

relationship: close denial that a son dies for his father's injustice
rationale: Ezekiel expressly says this obedient son will not die in his father's injustices. Deuteronomy prohibits sons dying for fathers and assigns death to each person's own sin. Ezekiel additionally describes the conduct by which this son lives.
source_text: and turned his hand from injustice, did not take interest or increase, practiced righteousness and walked in My commands. He will not die in his father’s injustices; he will surely live.

target_units.text: Fathers shall not die for children, and sons shall not die for fathers. Each shall die for his own sin.

relationship: close assignment of death to the wrongdoer's own sin
rationale: The oppressive father dies in his own injustice while the preceding son lives. Deuteronomy separates fathers' and sons' liability and says each dies for his own sin. The source illustrates that principle through this particular two-generation contrast.
source_text: But if his father practiced affliction and seized plunder, he did contrary things in the midst of My people and will die in his injustice.

target_units.text: Fathers shall not die for children, and sons shall not die for fathers. Each shall die for his own sin.

relationship: related righteousness and mercy joined with faithful conduct
rationale: The son's life is explained by his righteousness, mercy and observance of God's ordinances. Micah identifies doing justice, loving mercy and readiness to walk with God as what He seeks. The target does not address the source's disputed inheritance of a father's injustice.
source_text: You will say, ‘Why did the son not receive his father’s injustice?’ Because the son practiced righteousness and mercy, preserved all My ordinances and carried them out; he will surely live.

target_units.text: Has it been declared to you, O man, what is good? Or what does the Lord seek from you, except to do justice, and to love mercy, and to be ready to walk with the Lord your God?

relationship: close reciprocal exclusion of inherited liability for sin
rationale: Ezekiel says neither son nor father receives the other's injustice and that the sinning soul dies. Deuteronomy likewise denies both directions of substitution and says each dies for his own sin. The source also expressly assigns righteousness to the righteous person.
source_text: The soul that sins will die. The son will not receive his father’s injustice, nor the father his son’s injustice. The righteous person’s righteousness will be upon him, and the lawless person’s lawlessness upon him.

target_units.text: Fathers shall not die for children, and sons shall not die for fathers. Each shall die for his own sin.

relationship: close life promised to a wrongdoer who turns and practices righteousness
rationale: Both passages describe a lawless person turning, practicing judgment or righteousness and receiving life rather than death. The later passage adds restoration of pledges and seized property. The shared assurance concerns a changed course of conduct.
source_text: If the lawless person turns from all the lawlessness he committed, keeps all My commandments, and practices righteousness and mercy, he will surely live; he certainly will not die.

target_units.text: When I say to the impious man, “You will surely be put to death,” and he turns from his sin and practices judgment and righteousness,
and returns a pledge, repays what he seized and walks in the ordinances of life without doing wrong, he will surely live and certainly will not die.
None of the sins he committed will ever be remembered, because he practiced judgment and righteousness; in these he will live.

relationship: close promise not to remember sins
rationale: Ezekiel says the repentant person's transgressions will not be remembered. Jeremiah's new-covenant promise likewise says God will remember sins no more. The source expressly links the person's life to practiced righteousness, while the target places forgiveness within the new covenant.
source_text: None of the transgressions he committed will be remembered. By the righteousness he practiced, he will live.

target_units.text: And they will certainly not teach each his fellow citizen or his brother, saying, Know the Lord, because they will all know Me, from their least to their greatest. I will be merciful toward their injustices and certainly remember their sins no more.

relationship: close rejection of delight in the wrongdoer's death
rationale: Both declarations say God desires the wrongdoer to turn from his way and live rather than die. The later passage repeats this as an urgent address to Israel to turn completely.
source_text: Do I at all desire the death of the lawless, says the Lord, rather than his turning from his evil way and living?

target_units.text: Say to them, ‘I live, thus says the Lord: I do not desire the impious man’s death, but rather that he turn from his way and live. Turn back completely from your way! Why are you dying, house of Israel?’

relationship: related divine desire for repentance rather than destruction
rationale: Ezekiel contrasts death with turning and living. The letter explains the Lord's patience as not wishing anyone to perish but all to reach repentance. Its setting is the apparent delay of the promised coming, not Ezekiel's dispute over individual responsibility.
source_text: Do I at all desire the death of the lawless, says the Lord, rather than his turning from his evil way and living?

target_units.text: The Lord is not slow concerning the promise, as some consider slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing anyone to perish but all to come to repentance.

relationship: close warning that former righteousness does not excuse later lawlessness
rationale: Both passages say a formerly righteous person who commits lawlessness will not have his earlier righteous deeds remembered as protection. The later passage additionally describes trusting in one's righteousness. The warning does not declare that the earlier acts never happened.
source_text: But when a righteous person turns from his righteousness and practices injustice according to all the lawlessness the lawless person committed, none of the righteous acts he did will be remembered. In the transgression he committed and the sins he sinned, in these he will die.

target_units.text: Say to your people’s sons, ‘A righteous man’s righteousness certainly will not rescue him on the day he wanders, and an impious man’s lawlessness certainly will not harm him on the day he turns from it. A righteous man certainly will not be able to be saved.

When I speak to the righteous man—this one has trusted in his righteousness, yet commits lawlessness—none of his righteous deeds will ever be remembered. In the injustice he committed, in it he will die.

relationship: related affirmation of God's righteous ways against an accusation of unfairness
rationale: Ezekiel challenges the charge that God's way does not run straight. The song in Deuteronomy declares His works true, all His ways judgments and no unrighteousness in Him. The target affirms the divine righteousness questioned in the source without quoting that accusation.
source_text: You said, ‘The Lord’s way does not run straight.’ Hear now, the whole house of Israel: Surely My way does not fail to run straight? Is it not your way that fails to run straight?

target_units.text: God—true are His works, and all His ways are judgments; a faithful God, and there is no unrighteousness; righteous and holy is the Lord.

relationship: close repeated judgment on turning from righteousness to wrongdoing
rationale: Both statements describe a righteous person turning from righteousness, committing transgression or lawless deeds and dying in those acts. The correspondence preserves the source's emphasis on the person's changed conduct.
source_text: When the righteous person turns from his righteousness, commits a transgression and dies, in the transgression he committed—in it he will die.

target_units.text: When a righteous man turns from his righteousness and commits lawless deeds, he will die in them.

relationship: close preservation of life through turning from lawlessness
rationale: Ezekiel says the former wrongdoer who practices judgment and righteousness has preserved his life. The later statement says the sinner who turns and practices those things will live in them. Both connect life with the same reversal of practice.
source_text: When a lawless person turns from the lawlessness he practiced and practices judgment and righteousness, this one has preserved his life

target_units.text: When the sinner turns from his lawlessness and practices judgment and righteousness, in these he will live.

relationship: related mercy and life following abandonment of evil ways
rationale: Ezekiel promises certain life to the person who turns from his impieties. Isaiah calls the ungodly to forsake his ways and return to the Lord for mercy and abundant forgiveness. The source speaks in terms of life and death, while Isaiah names forgiveness explicitly.
source_text: and turned from all the impieties he committed; he will surely live, he certainly will not die.

target_units.text: let the ungodly forsake his ways, and the lawless man his counsels; and let him return to the Lord, and he will receive mercy; for He will abundantly forgive your sins.

relationship: close repeated charge and rebuttal concerning God's way
rationale: Both passages report the people saying God's way is not straight and answer that their own way is the defective one. The repeated disputation is more specific than a general assertion of divine justice.
source_text: The house of Israel says, ‘The Lord’s way does not go right.’ Surely My way does not fail to go right, house of Israel? Is it not your way that fails to go right?

target_units.text: Your people’s sons will say, “The Lord’s way is not straight.” Yet this way of theirs is not straight.

relationship: close individual judgment according to conduct
rationale: God says He will judge each Israelite according to his way. Romans says God will repay each according to his works, with the surrounding passage distinguishing good and evil conduct. The source also includes an immediate command to turn from impiety.
source_text: I will judge you, each according to his way, house of Israel, says the Lord. Turn back and turn away from all your impieties, and they will not become a punishment of injustice for you.

target_units.text: who will repay each according to his works:

relationship: related renewal of heart and spirit with differing forms of appeal
rationale: Ezekiel commands the people to make themselves a new heart and spirit. The psalm asks God to create a clean heart and renew an upright spirit within the speaker. The comparison preserves command and petition rather than assigning the same grammatical agency to both.
source_text: Cast away from yourselves all your impieties with which you acted impiously against Me, and make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit. Why are you dying, house of Israel?

target_units.text: Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew an upright spirit in my inward parts.

relationship: close new-heart and new-spirit language as command and divine promise
rationale: The people are commanded to make themselves a new heart and spirit. The later oracle promises that God will give a new heart and spirit and cause obedience to His ordinances. The common renewal language is explicit, while human command and divine gift remain distinguished.
source_text: Cast away from yourselves all your impieties with which you acted impiously against Me, and make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit. Why are you dying, house of Israel?

target_units.text: And I will give you a new heart, and I will give a new spirit within you; and I will take the heart of stone out of your flesh, and give you a heart of flesh.
I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My ordinances, keep My judgments and do them.

relationship: close denial that God desires or delights in death
rationale: Ezekiel says God does not desire the death of one who dies. Wisdom warns against pursuing death and says God neither made death nor delights in the living's destruction. The target adds a claim about death's origin that this source does not make.
source_text: For I do not desire the death of the one who dies, says the Lord.”

target_units.text: Do not pursue death through the wandering of your life, nor draw destruction upon yourselves through the works of your hands;
For God did not make death, neither does He delight in the destruction of the living.

relationship: parallel prophetic royal laments using animal imagery
rationale: Ezekiel is commanded to lament Israel's ruler, introducing the lion imagery that follows. The later command names Pharaoh and introduces lion and dragon images. The genre and figurative treatment of rulers correspond without identifying the two rulers.
source_text: “And you, take up a lament over Israel’s ruler,

target_units.text: “Son of man, take up a lament over Pharaoh, Egypt’s king, and say to him, ‘You were likened to a lion of nations, and you are like the dragon in the sea. You butted in your rivers, troubled water with your feet and trampled your rivers.

relationship: related lion-cub imagery in a royal family setting
rationale: The mother in the ruler's lament is called a cub and multiplies cubs among lions. Genesis calls Judah a lion's cub and follows it with language of rulers and leaders. The source's mother-as-cub wording is preserved rather than replaced with lioness or identified with the male Judah of the target.
source_text: and say: What was your mother? A cub! She came to be among lions; among lions she multiplied her cubs.

target_units.text: “Judah is a lion’s cub. From a shoot, my son, you have gone up. You reclined and slept as a lion, and as a cub; who shall rouse him?
“A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until the things reserved for him come; and he shall be the expectation of nations.

relationship: related predatory lion imagery for harmful rule
rationale: The ruler's cub becomes a lion that seizes prey and eats people. Proverbs compares a poor tyrant over a needy nation to a hungry lion and thirsty wolf. The common predatory rule does not imply identical images or describe Ezekiel's ruler as poor.
source_text: One of her cubs sprang away; he became a lion, learned to seize prey, and ate human beings.

target_units.text: One who tyrannizes over a needy nation while himself poor is a hungry lion and a thirsty wolf.

relationship: related forcible removal of a Judean ruler to Egypt
rationale: The lion is captured and led with a muzzle to Egypt. Kings narrates Joachas being removed from rule and brought by Pharaoh to Egypt. This offers a named instance of royal removal to that destination without assigning the unnamed lion a definitive historical identity.
source_text: Nations heard against him; he was caught in their destruction, and they led him with a muzzle to Egypt’s land.

target_units.text: Pharaoh Nechao removed him at Deblatha in Emath’s land so that he would not reign in Jerusalem. He imposed a penalty on the land of one hundred talents of silver and one hundred talents of gold.
Pharaoh Nechao made Eliakim, son of Josiah king of Judah, king over them in place of his father Josiah and changed his name to Joakim. He took Joachas and brought him into Egypt, and he died there.

relationship: close predatory lion imagery for rulers devouring lives
rationale: The cub becomes a lion, learns to seize prey and eats human beings. The later indictment likens leaders to roaring lions seizing prey and devouring lives. Both use lion predation to portray destructive leadership.
source_text: He moved among lions, became a lion, learned to seize prey, and ate human beings.

target_units.text: Her leaders within her are like roaring lions seizing prey, devouring lives with power, taking payments unjustly, and your widows have multiplied within you.

relationship: related devastation caused by roaring predatory leaders
rationale: The lion desolates cities and destroys the land through its roaring. The later oracle depicts roaring lion-like leaders devouring lives and multiplying widows. The source describes devastated territory, while the target states the harm to people more directly.
source_text: He fed in his boldness, desolated their cities, and destroyed the land and its fullness by the sound of his roaring.

target_units.text: Her leaders within her are like roaring lions seizing prey, devouring lives with power, taking payments unjustly, and your widows have multiplied within you.

relationship: close capture of an animal-figured ruler in the nations' nets
rationale: Nations spread nets over the lion and capture him. In the Pharaoh oracle God throws nets of many peoples over the animal-figured ruler. The agents' relation to God and the animal figures differ, but the political net imagery is particular.
source_text: Nations from the surrounding countries set themselves against him and spread their nets over him; he was caught in their destruction.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: I will throw nets of many peoples over you and haul you up with My hook,

relationship: related royal imprisonment under Babylon's king
rationale: The muzzled lion is brought to Babylon's king and prison so that its voice is no longer heard in Israel. Kings records a Judean king named Joakim being released from his prison house by Babylon's king. The target establishes a named Babylonian royal imprisonment without resolving which ruler Ezekiel's unnamed lion represents.
source_text: They put him in a muzzle and a cage. He came to Babylon’s king, and he brought him into prison, so that his voice would not be heard upon Israel’s mountains.

target_units.text: In the thirty-seventh year of the deportation of Joakim king of Judah, in the twelfth month, on the twenty-seventh of the month, Euilmarodach king of Babylon, in the year of his reign, lifted the head of Joakim king of Judah and brought him out of his prison house.

relationship: related fruitfulness of a plant supplied by water
rationale: The mother is compared to a vine and a pomegranate blossom, with fruit and shoot from abundant water. The psalm compares its righteous person to a tree beside waters yielding seasonal fruit. The source's maternal and national setting differs from the psalm's individual moral description.
source_text: Your mother was like a vine, like a blossom on a pomegranate tree, planted by water; her fruit and her shoot came from abundant water.

target_units.text: He will be like the tree planted beside the outlets of waters, which will give its fruit in its season, and whose leaf will not fall off; and everything he does will be prospered.

relationship: related rod-of-strength language associated with rule
rationale: The vine has a rod of strength for a tribe of leaders. The psalm speaks of the rod of power sent from Zion and commands dominion among enemies. The shared rod-and-rule association does not supply the source's full plant arrangement or identify its ruler with the psalm's addressee.
source_text: She had a rod of strength for a tribe of leaders; it rose in her size among the trunks, and it saw her size among the multitude of her branches.

target_units.text: The Lord will send out the rod of your power from Zion. Exercise dominion in the midst of your enemies.

relationship: close judgment through a scorching wind drying a vine
rationale: Both plant parables describe a scorching wind causing drying. The source adds being broken off, thrown to the ground and consumed by fire; the earlier parable specifically says the vine dries with its clod. The different added details are preserved.
source_text: She was broken off in wrath and thrown to the ground. The scorching wind dried her choice parts; her rod of strength was punished and dried up. Fire consumed her.

target_units.text: Behold, it grows fat—surely it will not prosper? Will it not dry up completely as soon as the scorching wind touches it? It will dry up together with the clod of its growth.’”

relationship: related image of a plant consigned to wilderness
rationale: Ezekiel's mother-vine is planted in a waterless wilderness. Jeremiah compares one who trusts human strength with a tamarisk dwelling in wilderness and uninhabited salt land. The environments communicate deprivation, without assigning Jeremiah's exact individual offense to the source's maternal figure.
source_text: Now they have planted her in the wilderness, in a waterless land,

target_units.text: and he will be like a wild tamarisk in the wilderness; he will not see when good things come, and will dwell among salt-plants and in a wilderness, in a salt land that is not inhabited.

relationship: related royal plant parables ending in fire from within the vegetation
rationale: Fire comes from a rod of the vine's choice parts and devours it, leaving no rod of strength. The bramble offered kingship threatens fire from itself to consume Lebanon's cedars. The common self-originating destructive fire belongs to different political plant parables and different plant species.
source_text: and fire went out from a rod of her choice parts and devoured her, and there was no rod of strength in her. A tribe is for a parable of lament, and it will become a lament.”

target_units.text: And the bramble said to the trees, ‘If in truth you anoint me king over you, come and trust in my shelter. But if not, let fire come forth from the bramble and consume the cedars of Lebanon.’

relationship: close scene of Israel's elders sitting before the prophet
rationale: Ezekiel records elders coming to inquire of the Lord and sitting before him. The earlier scene likewise has men from Israel's elders coming and sitting before him, followed by God's challenge to their approach. The earlier passage supplies no corresponding date.
source_text: In the seventh year, in the fifth month, on the tenth of the month, men from the elders of the house of Israel came to question the Lord and sat before me.

target_units.text: Men from Israel’s elders came to me and sat before me.

relationship: parallel divine challenge to the elders' consultation
rationale: The Lord challenges the elders' coming to question Him and refuses to answer. The earlier oracle questions whether He should answer men who set thoughts upon their hearts and the punishment of their injustices before their faces. Its following verses describe an answer in their entanglement, so the two responses are not presented as identical.
source_text: “Son of man, speak to Israel’s elders and say to them, ‘Thus says the Lord: Have you come to question Me? As I live, I will certainly not answer you, says the Lord.’

target_units.text: “Son of man, these men have set their thoughts upon their hearts and set the punishment of their injustices before their faces. Shall I indeed answer them?

relationship: related historical indictment of the fathers' disobedience
rationale: Ezekiel is told to testify to the fathers' lawlessness before the historical recital. The prayer in Nehemiah confesses the fathers' arrogant refusal to hear commandments and their attempted return to Egyptian slavery. It supplies an example of the same ancestral indictment in a penitential prayer rather than this prophetic challenge.
source_text: Shall I indeed exact retribution upon them? Son of man, solemnly testify to them about their fathers’ lawlessness,

target_units.text: “But they and our fathers acted arrogantly, stiffened their necks and did not listen to Thy commandments.

“They refused to listen and did not remember Thy wonders that Thou hadst done among them. They stiffened their necks and appointed leadership to return to their slavery in Egypt. But Thou art a merciful and compassionate God, longsuffering and abundant in mercy, and Thou didst not abandon them.

relationship: close declaration of Israel's God in the Egyptian deliverance setting
rationale: Ezekiel recalls God's choosing Israel and becoming known to Jacob's house in Egypt as the Lord their God. Exodus promises deliverance from Egypt, taking Israel as God's people and their knowing Him as the Lord their God. The source's supporting hand is not converted into an unstated oath.
source_text: and say to them, ‘Thus says the Lord: From the day I chose the house of Israel, I became known to the seed of Jacob’s house and was known to them in Egypt’s land. I supported them with My hand, saying, “I am the Lord your God.”

target_units.text: Go, say to the sons of Israel: ‘I am the Lord. I will bring you out from the Egyptians’ domination and deliver you from slavery. I will ransom you with an uplifted arm and with great judgment.
And I will take you to Myself for a people, and I will be your God; and you shall know that I am the Lord your God, who brought you out from the oppression of the Egyptians.

relationship: close promise of departure from Egypt into milk-and-honey land
rationale: Both passages describe God bringing Israel out of Egypt into a land flowing with milk and honey. Exodus calls it good and spacious and names its peoples; Ezekiel additionally compares it to a honeycomb relative to all the earth.
source_text: On that day I supported them with My hand to bring them out of Egypt’s land into the land I prepared for them, a land flowing with milk and honey; it is a honeycomb compared with all the earth.

target_units.text: I have come down to rescue them from the hand of the Egyptians and bring them out of that land into a good and spacious land, a land flowing with milk and honey, to the place of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Girgashites, Hivites, and Jebusites.

relationship: close rejection of Egyptian practices
rationale: Ezekiel recalls the command to cast away abominations and avoid Egypt's practices. Leviticus forbids following the practices of the land of Egypt where Israel lived, also naming Canaan. This particular rejected model of conduct is explicit in both.
source_text: I said to them, “Let each cast away the abominations of his eyes, and do not be defiled by Egypt’s practices. I am the Lord your God.”

target_units.text: You shall not follow the practices of the land of Egypt, where you dwelt; and you shall not follow the practices of the land of Canaan, where I am bringing you; neither shall you walk in their statutes.

relationship: related ancestral rebellion associated with Egypt
rationale: Ezekiel describes disobedience and refusal to abandon Egyptian practices. The psalm confesses ancestral sin and says the fathers in Egypt failed to understand God's wonders and provoked Him at the Red Sea. The episodes share Egyptian setting and rebellion while describing different specific acts.
source_text: They revolted from Me and would not listen to Me. They did not cast away the abominations of their eyes or abandon Egypt’s practices. I said I would pour My wrath upon them and complete My anger in them in the midst of Egypt’s land.

target_units.text: We sinned with our fathers; we acted lawlessly and unjustly.
Our fathers in Egypt did not understand Thy wonders; they did not remember the abundance of Thy mercy and provoked Thee while going up in the Red Sea.

relationship: close preservation of the people for God's name
rationale: Ezekiel says God acted so His name would not be profaned among the nations who witnessed their departure from Egypt. The psalm says He saved them for His name's sake to make His might known. The shared stated motive is more particular than deliverance alone.
source_text: I acted so that My name would not be profaned at all before the nations among whom they are, among whom I was known to them before their eyes by bringing them out of Egypt’s land.

target_units.text: He saved them for His name’s sake, to make His might known.

relationship: close historical movement from Egypt into the wilderness
rationale: God recalls bringing the people out of Egypt into the wilderness. Exodus narrates His leading them by the wilderness road toward the Red Sea. The target specifies that route without adding it to Ezekiel's shorter recollection.
source_text: I brought them out of Egypt’s land and brought them into the wilderness,

target_units.text: God led the people around by the road into the wilderness toward the Red Sea. The sons of Israel went up from the land of Egypt in the fifth generation.

relationship: close ordinance-and-life formulation
rationale: Ezekiel says God gave ordinances which a person who does them will live by. Leviticus uses the same connection between doing God's ordinances and judgments and living by them. Ezekiel places this lawgiving within the wilderness history.
source_text: and gave them My commands and made My ordinances known to them, which a person will carry out and by which he will live.

target_units.text: And you shall keep all My ordinances and all My judgments, and do them; the man who does them shall live by them; I am the Lord your God.

relationship: close Sabbath sign identifying the Lord who sanctifies Israel
rationale: Both passages say the Sabbaths are a sign between God and Israel so that they may know He is the Lord who sanctifies them. The explicit purpose of the Sabbath sign is the central correspondence.
source_text: I gave them My sabbaths as a sign between Me and them, so that they might know that I am the Lord who sanctifies them.

target_units.text: “Command the sons of Israel, saying, ‘See that you keep My Sabbaths, for they are a sign with Me and among you throughout your generations, that you may know that I am the Lord who sanctifies you.

relationship: related wilderness Sabbath violation followed by judgment
rationale: Ezekiel accuses Israel of greatly profaning Sabbaths in the wilderness and recalls threatened wrath. Numbers narrates a specific man gathering wood on a Sabbath in the wilderness and the sentence carried out against him. The individual case illustrates the type of breach without equating his execution with the source's threatened destruction of the people.
source_text: I said to the house of Israel in the wilderness, “Walk in My commands.” But they did not walk, and they rejected My ordinances, which a person will carry out and by which he will live; they greatly profaned My sabbaths. I said I would pour My wrath upon them in the wilderness to consume them utterly.

target_units.text: And while the sons of Israel were in the wilderness, they found a man gathering wood on the Sabbath day.
And those who found him gathering wood on the Sabbath day brought him unto Moses, Aaron, and the whole congregation of the sons of Israel.
And they placed him in custody, because they had not determined what they should do to him.
And the Lord spoke unto Moses, saying: The man must certainly be put to death. Stone him with stones, all the congregation.
And the whole congregation brought him outside the camp, and the whole congregation stoned him with stones outside the camp, as the Lord had commanded Moses.

relationship: related preservation of Israel in view of God's reputation before Egypt
rationale: Ezekiel gives God's avoiding profanation of His name before the witnessing nations as the reason for His action. Moses appeals to what the Egyptians might say about the Exodus if God destroys Israel, and God is appeased. The target presents an intercessor's appeal rather than Ezekiel's direct divine explanation.
source_text: I acted so that My name would not be profaned at all before the nations from whom I brought them out before their eyes.

target_units.text: Moses entreated the Lord God and said, “Why, O Lord, art Thou angry with Thy people, whom Thou didst lead out of the land of Egypt with great strength and Thine uplifted arm?
Let not the Egyptians say, ‘He led them out with evil intent, to kill them in the mountains and consume them from the earth.’ Cease from Thy fierce anger and be merciful concerning Thy people’s evil,

remembering Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, Thy servants, to whom Thou didst swear by Thyself and speak, saying, ‘I will greatly multiply your seed as the stars of heaven in multitude’; and all this land which Thou didst say Thou wouldest give to their seed, they shall possess for ever.”
The Lord was appeased concerning the calamity He had said He would bring upon His people.

relationship: close exclusion of the wilderness rebels from the promised land
rationale: Ezekiel recalls God's raised hand against bringing the generation into the good land. Numbers records the sworn sentence that the grumblers' bodies will fall in the wilderness and they will not enter the land. The target names exceptions and specifies those counted from twenty years old.
source_text: I too raised My hand against them in the wilderness, that I would not bring them at all into the land I gave them, a land flowing with milk and honey, a honeycomb compared with all the earth,

target_units.text: Say to them, I live, says the Lord: I will certainly do to you just as you have spoken into My ears.
In this wilderness your bodies shall fall, with your entire registration and those of you counted from twenty years old and upward who grumbled against Me.
You shall certainly not enter the land over which I stretched out My hand to settle you upon it, except Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun.

relationship: related rejection of inwardly directed infidelity and neglected commandments
rationale: Ezekiel connects rejected ordinances and profaned Sabbaths with hearts following their reflections. Numbers commands remembrance of God's laws and forbids turning after one's thoughts and eyes in prostitution. The target provides a corrective to that inward misdirection without supplying Ezekiel's Sabbath accusation.
source_text: because they rejected My ordinances, did not walk in My commands, and were profaning My sabbaths, and they followed the reflections of their hearts.

target_units.text: And it shall be among your fringes; and you shall see them, and remember all the commandments of the Lord, and do them; and you shall not turn aside after your thoughts and after your eyes, after which you go a whoring,
that you may remember and do all My commandments, and be holy unto your God.

relationship: close divine preservation despite wilderness rebellion
rationale: Ezekiel says God's eye spared the people and He did not make a complete end of them in the wilderness. The historical prayer says His compassion did not abandon them there and recounts continued guidance and nourishment. These specified provisions illustrate preservation but are not listed in the source unit.
source_text: My eye spared them from obliteration, and I did not make a complete end of them in the wilderness.

target_units.text: “Thou, in Thine abundant compassion, didst not abandon them in the wilderness. Thou didst not turn the pillar of cloud away from them by day, to guide them on the way, or the pillar of fire by night, to light for them the way they should travel.
“Thou gavest Thy good Spirit to give them understanding. Thou didst not withhold Thy manna from their mouths, and Thou gavest them water for their thirst.
“For forty years Thou didst nourish them in the wilderness; they lacked nothing. Their garments did not grow old, and their feet did not split open.

relationship: close warning not to imitate the fathers' evil practices
rationale: Ezekiel tells the children not to walk in their fathers' ordinances or become defiled by their practices. Zechariah likewise warns against becoming like the fathers who ignored calls to leave evil ways and practices. The target describes former prophetic warnings rather than the source's wilderness speech to children.
source_text: I said to their children in the wilderness, “Do not walk in your fathers’ ordinances, do not keep their judgments, do not mix yourselves with their practices, and do not be defiled.

target_units.text: Do not become like your fathers, against whom the former prophets brought charges, saying, ‘Thus says the Lord Almighty: Turn away from your evil ways and your evil practices.’ But they did not listen attentively to Me, says the Lord.

relationship: close command to carry out God's own judgments and ordinances
rationale: God identifies Himself and commands walking in His commands and doing His ordinances. Leviticus likewise requires doing His judgments and keeping and walking in His ordinances, identifying Him as the Lord their God. This contrasts with following the fathers' practices in the preceding source unit.
source_text: I am the Lord your God. Walk in My commands, keep My ordinances and carry them out,

target_units.text: You shall do My judgments, and keep My ordinances, to walk in them; I am the Lord your God.

relationship: close Sabbath observance as a sign between God and Israel
rationale: Ezekiel commands sanctifying the Sabbaths as a sign between God and the people. Exodus commands their continuing observance and calls the Sabbath an everlasting sign between God and Israel. The target additionally explains the sign through creation and divine rest.
source_text: and sanctify My sabbaths; let it be a sign between Me and you, so that you may know that I am the Lord your God.”

target_units.text: The sons of Israel shall keep the Sabbaths, observing them throughout their generations: an everlasting covenant.
It is an everlasting sign between Me and the sons of Israel, for in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day He ceased and rested.’”

relationship: close disobedience to life-giving ordinances despite divine testimony
rationale: Ezekiel says the children failed to keep the ordinances by which the one doing them lives. Nehemiah's prayer repeats that life-giving-law formulation while confessing refusal to listen and recounting God's repeated testimony. It does not separately identify these people as Ezekiel's wilderness children or expressly mention their Sabbath profanation in this range.
source_text: Their children too embittered Me. They did not walk in My commands or keep My ordinances to carry them out, which a person will carry out and by which he will live; they were profaning My sabbaths. I said I would pour My wrath upon them in the wilderness and complete My anger upon them.

target_units.text: “Thou didst testify to them to turn them back to Thy law, but they did not listen. Instead, they sinned against Thy commandments and judgments, which, if a person does them, that person will live by them. They presented a disobedient back, stiffened their necks and did not listen.
“Thou didst prolong Thy dealings with them for many years and testify to them by Thy Spirit through Thy prophets, but they did not give ear. Thou gavest them into the hand of the peoples of the land.

relationship: related restraint from destruction in view of the nations' perception
rationale: God recalls acting to avoid profaning His name before those who saw the Exodus. Moses' plea similarly invokes the Egyptians' possible account of a destructive Exodus, after which God is appeased concerning the threatened calamity. The source gives the divine motive, while the target narrates the intercession.
source_text: I acted so that My name would not be profaned at all before the nations from whom I brought them out before their eyes.

target_units.text: Moses entreated the Lord God and said, “Why, O Lord, art Thou angry with Thy people, whom Thou didst lead out of the land of Egypt with great strength and Thine uplifted arm?
Let not the Egyptians say, ‘He led them out with evil intent, to kill them in the mountains and consume them from the earth.’ Cease from Thy fierce anger and be merciful concerning Thy people’s evil,

remembering Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, Thy servants, to whom Thou didst swear by Thyself and speak, saying, ‘I will greatly multiply your seed as the stars of heaven in multitude’; and all this land which Thou didst say Thou wouldest give to their seed, they shall possess for ever.”
The Lord was appeased concerning the calamity He had said He would bring upon His people.

relationship: close raised-hand sentence of scattering among nations
rationale: Ezekiel recalls lifting His hand in the wilderness to scatter the people among nations and countries. The psalm likewise says God lifted His hand to cast them down in the wilderness and scatter their offspring among nations and countries. The psalm explicitly distinguishes the original generation from its offspring.
source_text: I raised My hand against them in the wilderness, to scatter them among the nations and disperse them among the countries,

target_units.text: He lifted His hand to them, to cast them down in the wilderness,
and to cast their offspring down among the nations, and scatter them in the countries.

relationship: related turning of the eyes from God's commandments
rationale: Ezekiel connects rejection of judgments, commands and Sabbaths with eyes following the fathers' reflections. Numbers commands remembering and doing the commandments rather than turning after one's thoughts and eyes. The target does not name the fathers' practices or mention Sabbaths in these verses.
source_text: because they did not carry out My ordinances, rejected My commands and were profaning My sabbaths, while their eyes followed their fathers’ reflections.

target_units.text: And it shall be among your fringes; and you shall see them, and remember all the commandments of the Lord, and do them; and you shall not turn aside after your thoughts and after your eyes, after which you go a whoring,
that you may remember and do all My commandments, and be holy unto your God.

relationship: contrasting statements concerning gifts and womb-opening firstborn
rationale: Ezekiel speaks of defilement through gifts when God passes through every womb-opener, with destruction as the stated purpose. Exodus commands consecration of every womb-opening firstborn as God's own. The particular firstborn language is related, without defining Ezekiel's passing-through clause as an explicit statement about burning children.
source_text: I will defile them through their gifts, when I pass through every one who opens the womb, so that I may destroy them.

target_units.text: “Consecrate to Me every firstborn, the first offspring opening every womb among the sons of Israel, both human and animal. It is Mine.”

relationship: close sacrifices on heights and beneath shady trees
rationale: Ezekiel describes sacrifice, fragrant offerings and libations at high hills and shady trees. Hosea likewise names sacrifices on mountaintops and hills beneath trees that provide shade. The target names particular trees and adds consequences for the daughters and daughters-in-law.
source_text: I brought them into the land I raised My hand to give them. They saw every high hill and every shady tree; there they sacrificed to their gods, there they set a fragrant aroma, and there they poured their libations.

target_units.text: On the mountaintops they sacrificed, and on the hills they offered sacrifice, beneath oak, poplar and a tree providing shade, because shelter is good. Therefore your daughters will prostitute themselves and your daughters-in-law commit adultery.

relationship: related renewal of the fathers' corrupt religious practices
rationale: Ezekiel accuses the people of being defiled in their fathers' manner and prostituting themselves in their abominations. Judges describes people returning after a judge's death to corruption worse than their fathers', following other gods and retaining their practices. The source does not name the death of a judge as its trigger.
source_text: Therefore say to the house of Israel, ‘Thus says the Lord: Are you being defiled in your fathers’ lawlessness and prostituting yourselves after their abominations?

target_units.text: When the judge died, they turned back and again acted more corruptly than their fathers, following other gods to serve them and bow down to them. They did not cast away their practices or depart from their hard way.

relationship: related refusal to hear worshippers while wrongdoing persists
rationale: Ezekiel joins continuing defilement through offerings and reflections with God's refusal to answer inquiry. Isaiah says God will turn His eyes away and not hear multiplied supplication because the people's hands are full of blood. The rejected approaches and specified offenses differ while the incompatibility of persistent wrongdoing and an expected favorable hearing is shared.
source_text: In the firstfruits of your gifts, in your separations, you are being defiled with all your reflections to this very day. Shall I answer you, house of Israel? As I live, says the Lord, I will certainly not answer you, nor will this rise upon your spirit.

target_units.text: Whenever you stretch your hands toward Me, I will turn My eyes away from you. Even if you multiply supplication, I will not listen to you, for your hands are full of blood.

relationship: close wood-and-stone worship language with different announced outcomes
rationale: Ezekiel rejects the people's plan to become like the nations by serving wood and stone. Deuteronomy warns that dispersion will lead to serving human-made gods of wood and stone. The objects of worship correspond; the source's rejection of their plan is not treated as the target's identical predicted outcome.
source_text: It will not be as you say: “We will be like the nations and like the tribes of the earth, serving woods and stones.”

target_units.text: And the Lord shall scatter you among all the nations, and you shall be left few in number among the nations whither the Lord shall bring you.
And there you shall serve other gods, the works of men’s hands, wood and stone, which shall neither see, nor hear, nor eat, nor smell.

relationship: close mighty-hand and uplifted-arm language for divine action
rationale: Ezekiel announces God's reign through a mighty hand, uplifted arm and outpoured wrath. Deuteronomy recalls the mighty hand and uplifted arm by which God took a nation out of Egypt. The source applies this forceful language to His rule over Israel rather than simply repeating the Exodus event.
source_text: Therefore, as I live, says the Lord, with a mighty hand, a high arm and outpoured wrath I will reign over you.

target_units.text: Or has God attempted to go and take unto Himself a nation from the midst of a nation, by trial, and by signs, and by wonders, and by war, and by a mighty hand, and by an uplifted arm, and by great visions, according to all that the Lord our God did in Egypt before your eyes?

relationship: close gathering from peoples and countries
rationale: God promises to bring the people out from the peoples and gather them from countries where they were scattered. The later oracle likewise gathers from nations and countries and brings them into their own land. The source additionally names mighty hand, uplifted arm and wrath.
source_text: I will bring you out from the peoples and receive you from the countries where you were scattered, with a mighty hand, a high arm and outpoured wrath.

target_units.text: I will take you out of the nations, gather you out of all the lands and bring you into your own land.

relationship: related divine encounter after placement in a wilderness
rationale: Ezekiel announces being brought to the wilderness of the peoples for face-to-face contention. Hosea's feminine figure is placed in a wilderness where God speaks to her heart, with the Exodus recalled. The wilderness encounter corresponds while contention and the target's promised possessions and understanding are distinguished.
source_text: I will bring you into the wilderness of the peoples and contend with you there, face to face.

target_units.text: “Therefore look, I am leading her astray; I will place her in a wilderness and speak to her heart,
and from there I will give her her possessions and the Valley of Achor to open her understanding. There she will be humbled as in the days of her infancy and the days of her ascent from Egypt’s land.

relationship: related wilderness contention with the rebellious ancestors
rationale: Ezekiel says the coming contention will resemble His contention with the fathers in Egypt's wilderness. Numbers records God's challenge to the people's persistent provocation and unbelief and His threatened destruction. The target supplies a concrete wilderness judgment scene without claiming the source uniquely names this episode.
source_text: As I contended with your fathers in the wilderness of Egypt’s land, so I will judge you, says the Lord.

target_units.text: And the Lord said unto Moses: How long will this people provoke Me? How long will they refuse to believe Me, despite all the signs I have done among them?
I will strike them with death and destroy them, and I will make you and your father’s house into a nation greater and much more numerous than this one.

relationship: close passing beneath a staff in a count
